content: Ischaemic reperfusion injury is a condition that can result in kidney dysfunction or even kidney failure. Ischaemic preconditioning is a technique that involves a brief period of restricted blood flow to specific organs or tissues, followed by a restoration of blood flow. This method has been proposed as a potential strategy to protect the kidneys from damage caused by ischaemia reperfusion injury. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of both local and remote ischaemic preconditioning in reducing ischaemia reperfusion injury in individuals experiencing renal ischaemia reperfusion injury. The review included randomized controlled trials that assessed kidney function and the role of ischaemic preconditioning in patients undergoing surgical procedures known to cause kidney injury. However, studies involving kidney transplantation were excluded. The data collection process involved assessing the eligibility and quality of studies, with two independent authors extracting data. Information was gathered on study characteristics, such as the type of surgery, the protocol for remote ischaemic preconditioning, and the type of anesthesia used. Primary outcomes included serum creatinine levels and adverse effects related to remote ischaemic preconditioning. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of acute kidney injury, the need for dialysis, levels of neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, length of hospital stay, and mortality. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) along with their 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 28 studies involving 6,851 patients were included in the review. The risk of bias was assessed as unclear to low for most studies. High-quality evidence indicated that remote ischaemic preconditioning had little to no effect on reducing serum creatinine levels on postoperative days one, two, and three when compared to control groups. Specifically, the mean differences in serum creatinine levels were as follows: day one (MD -0.02 mg/dL, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.02), day two (MD -0.04 mg/dL, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.02), and day three (MD -0.05 mg/dL, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.10). Serious adverse events were reported in four patients who underwent remote ischaemic preconditioning via iliac clamping. However, the evidence regarding whether remote ischaemic preconditioning using cuff inflation increases adverse effects was of low certainty. Among 15 studies involving 3,993 participants, the risk ratio for adverse effects was 3.47 (95% CI 0.55 to 21.76), but only two studies reported any adverse effects (6/1,999 in the remote ischaemic preconditioning group versus 1/1,994 in the control group). The remaining 13 studies reported no adverse effects in either group. Remote ischaemic preconditioning showed little to no effect on the need for dialysis (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.94; moderate-quality evidence), length of hospital stay (MD 0.17 days, 95% CI -0.46 to 0.80; high-quality evidence), or all-cause mortality (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.37; high-quality evidence). There was some evidence suggesting a slight improvement in the incidence of acute kidney injury when assessed using the AKIN criteria (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.00; high-quality evidence) or the RIFLE criteria (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.12; moderate-quality evidence). In conclusion, remote ischaemic preconditioning using cuff inflation appears to be a safe method. However, it likely results in little to no difference in serum creatinine levels, adverse effects, the need for dialysis, length of hospital stay, mortality, or the incidence of acute kidney injury. While the evidence was of moderate to high certainty, the available data do not confirm the efficacy of remote ischaemic preconditioning in reducing renal ischaemia reperfusion injury in patients undergoing major cardiac and vascular surgeries where such injury may occur.
